reason: The sources provide multi-site documentation from Wikipedia, ESO, NASA, NOIRLab, and Astronomy.com to verify over a dozen precise claims about the M87 black hole image.
story: On April 10, 2019, astronomers revealed humanity's first direct image of a black hole: the supermassive beast M87*, lurking 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. Packing 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun into a single cosmic abyss, its event horizon spans nearly 40 billion kilometers—easily dwarfing our entire solar system. Because black holes swallow all light, the object itself is invisible. Instead, telescopes captured its dark shadow silhouetted against a swirling, incandescent ring of matter whipped to near light-speed. Capturing this cosmic silhouette required the Event Horizon Telescope, a global network of eight radio observatories synchronized with atomic clocks to effectively turn planet Earth into one giant virtual dish. The resulting image confirmed Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity under the universe's most extreme gravitational conditions, proving that what once seemed mathematically impossible could finally be seen.
angle: To photograph an event horizon 55 million light-years away, scientists turned planet Earth into an observatory—capturing a 40-billion-kilometer black hole that could swallow our entire solar system whole.

claims.claim: Messier 87 hosts a supermassive black hole with an estimated mass of 6.5 billion times that of our Sun.
The first direct image of a black hole and its shadow was unveiled to the public on April 10, 2019.
Messier 87 is a supergiant elliptical galaxy situated in the Virgo galaxy cluster.
The Event Horizon Telescope combined independent radio stations across the globe to act as an Earth-sized virtual telescope using very-long-baseline interferometry.
The landmark 2017 observations of M87 were conducted using eight ground-based radio observatories distributed across the planet.
Participating radio telescopes synchronized their recorded data using ultra-precise atomic clocks.
Because raw observational data was too vast for the internet, petabytes of data were stored on hard drives and physically flown by airplanes to central processing centers.
Data correlation and supercomputing image processing were conducted at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy and MIT Haystack Observatory.
The initial historic observation of the black hole was conducted at a radio wavelength of 1.3 millimeters.
The planetary array achieved an angular resolving power of roughly 20 microarcseconds.
The event horizon of the M87 black hole spans approximately 40 billion kilometers across.
The black hole casts a central shadow that is approximately 2.5 times larger than the physical event horizon boundary.
The crescent ring around the shadow exhibits asymmetric brightness because material rotating toward the observer is intensified by relativistic beaming.
The discovery results and image analysis were published in a dedicated series of six papers in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
The captured shadow matched theoretical models of a spinning Kerr black hole, providing direct confirmation of Einstein's general theory of relativity.
Messier 87 launches an energetic plasma jet traveling at relativistic speeds that extends roughly 5,000 light-years into space.
The astronomical observing campaign that gathered the primary data for the image occurred in April 2017.
The University of Arizona 12-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak was subsequently upgraded and added to expand the Event Horizon Telescope array.

disputed: Distance to Messier 87: Sources S1 and S7 cite approximately 53 to 53.5 million light-years, while S3 and S4 cite 55 million light-years. Scripts should state 'roughly 53 to 55 million light-years'.

Displacement of the black hole from the galactic center: A 2010 study suggested an offset of 23 light-years, but subsequent 2011 and 2018 studies determined this was an artifact of variable jet brightness. Scripts should omit this debunked offset.

Photon ring detection claim: An August 2022 remastered analysis claimed to resolve the fundamental photon ring signature of M87*, but this result was formally disputed by other astronomers. Scripts should attribute or omit this claim.
